title: Karam appointed Christian qaimaqam of Mount Lebanon
why: Youssef Bey Karam held the northern Christian qaimaqamate until the 1861 Règlement; he later resisted the mutasarrifate that replaced it.

title: Draft Règlement for Mount Lebanon dated by the Powers
why: Draft text amended by agreement and then enacted by firman; fixed a Christian governor with the title Mushir, seated at Deir el Qamar.

title: Règlement Organique and Beyoglu Protocol create the Mutasarrifate
why: Ends the double qaimaqamate; Mount Lebanon becomes an autonomous sanjak under an Ottoman Christian governor backed by five European powers.

title: Daoud Pasha nominated first mutasarrif of Mount Lebanon
why: Armenian Catholic Ottoman official named for three years; he built the council, courts and tax system set by the Règlement.

title: Administrative council of twelve set up under the Règlement
why: Four Maronite, three Druze, two Greek Orthodox, one each Sunni, Shia and Melkite members advise on taxes and imports (other sources differ on seats).

title: Feudal privileges abolished; equality before the law proclaimed
why: The Règlement ended the muqata'ji tax-farming privileges of local lords, a break with the emirate order.

title: Security: Lebanese gendarmerie inside, Ottoman troops on Damascus road
why: Article 14 split policing: locals kept the Mountain, Ottoman soldiers guarded the Beirut-Damascus and Sidon-Tripoli roads.

title: French troops hold Beirut and parts of Mount Lebanon until mid-1861
why: The 1860 French expedition stayed until the new statute was in place.

title: Daoud Pasha exiles Karam to Turkey
why: Karam refused the non-native governor and demanded home rule; he stayed abroad until 1864.

title: Daoud Pasha's term mandated for three years as a trial
why: The Protocol set a trial period to 1864, after which he reported on the system to Istanbul.

title: Daoud Pasha builds the administration: officials, elected sheikhs, census, land survey
why: He appointed department heads, ran village elections, counted the population, surveyed land and collected Bekaa revenue for the Mountain.

title: Karam allowed back to Ehden; campaigns against the mutasarrifate
why: He called for ending the autonomous system, abolishing levies and moving Ottoman troops out.

title: Revised Règlement Organique signed, making the statute permanent
why: Eighteen articles; added a Maronite district; council reset to 4 Maronite, 3 Druze, 3 Orthodox and Greek Catholic, 1 Sunni, 1 Shia. Stood until 1914.

title: Daoud Pasha's mandate renewed for five years
why: The Porte accepted part of his proposed changes and extended him to 1868-69.

title: Karam's men and Ottoman troops clash at Maameltein
why: Start of the 1866 Karam revolt; Karam was at Mass when regulars attacked his men; he wrote to Istanbul and the Powers.

title: Amine Pasha enters Zgharta with 3,800 troops
why: Ottoman force sent against Karam took over his house and burned many houses before leaving on 25 January.

title: Karam meets Amine Pasha at Karmsaddeh and submits his sword
why: Amine Pasha saw no revolt but Daoud Pasha refused any settlement, so the fighting resumed.

title: Battle of Bnachii between Karam's men and government forces
why: Largest clash of the revolt; the source gives it as a 12-hour fight won by Karam and gives ~1,000 enemy losses (partisan-leaning account).

title: Karam revolt: clash at Sebhel
why: One of a series of 1866 engagements listed for Karam against Ottoman forces.

title: Karam revolt: clashes at Ehmej and Anaya
why: Fighting in Jbeil district during the Karam rising.

title: Karam revolt: clash at Wadi en-Nousour
why: Another 1866 engagement between Karam's men and the mutasarrif's forces.

title: Karam revolt: clashes at Aitou and Kfarfou
why: Fighting spreads across the northern Mount Lebanon highlands.

title: Karam revolt: clash at Hadath
why: The revolt reaches the Beirut hinterland.

title: Karam revolt: clashes at Ayn el Jawz and Bchenata
why: Continued 1866 engagements.

title: Karam revolt: clashes at Ayn Karna and Wadi Miziara
why: Last engagement in the page's battle list before Karam's exile.

title: Youssef Karam leads revolt against the Mutasarrifate
why: Rebellion of 1866-67 against Ottoman rule and Daoud Pasha, read by some as an early expression of Lebanese nationalism.

title: Karam leaves Lebanon on a French ship for Algeria
why: At Bkerke the French consul, in Napoleon III's name, told him to leave in return for guarantees for his men.

title: Ottoman municipal code issued for the provinces
why: Basis for municipalities such as Beirut's; revised in 1877.

title: Daoud Pasha resigns; Franko Pasha becomes mutasarrif
why: Daoud's resignation bid for more territory (Beirut, Sidon, Bekaa) was accepted at once; Nasri Franko Coussa succeeded him.

title: Beirut municipality established with Ahmad Pasha Abdza as president
why: Municipal government for the city, created under Tanzimat law; it later went into debt to French banks.

title: Franko Pasha era: calm, schools, students sent to Europe
why: He gave up the Bekaa tax to the Porte and cut staff pay 10%; the source says bribery grew afterwards.

title: Hadiqat al-Akhbar again semi-official under Franko Pasha
why: The Beirut weekly acted as a quasi-official paper in 1869-70 (it had held that role since 1860).

title: Exiled Karam publishes appeal to European governments
why: Rome pamphlet, one of several he issued 1871-77 against those who had let him down.

title: Franko Pasha dies; Rustem Pasha appointed mutasarrif
why: Rustem Mariani, formerly Ottoman ambassador in Moscow, governed to 1883, wintering in Beirut.

title: Rustem Pasha raises taxes, opens schools and roads; dispute with archbishop
why: Budget deficit led to pay cuts and higher taxes; he clashed with Archbishop Pierre al-Bustani, exiled to Jerusalem then restored (exact year not given, 1873-83). (corrected from 1873: 1873-1883 is Rustem's term; events are undated within it)

title: First Ottoman parliament meets; Mount Lebanon sends no deputy
why: Autonomous status was the reason given; the same argument returned in 1908.

title: Municipal Code for the provinces replaces the 1867 code
why: Introduced elected municipal councils; Beirut's first municipal elections followed.

title: Rustem Pasha not renewed; Wasa Pasha (Vaso Pashë) becomes mutasarrif
why: Lebanese and French objected to renewal; Wasa, a Catholic Albanian writer, governed to 1892.

title: Wasa Pasha builds Beiteddine hospital and Baabda and Zahle seraglios
why: Baabda became the permanent winter seat; he also built roads, bridges and first excavated antiquities (years within 1883-92).

title: Ottoman census prelim: Beirut vilayet-area population 533,500
why: Results published only in 1908; the region (later Beirut vilayet) ranked fourth most populous of 36 provinces.

title: Beirut made capital of a new vilayet
why: Carved from the Syria vilayet; sanjaks Latakia, Tripoli, Beirut, Acre and (per one source) Nablus/Bekaa; by 1907 Beirut handled 11% of Ottoman foreign trade.

title: Official Beirut vilayet gazette Bayrut appears
why: Listed in the Arabic periodicals chronology for 1888.

title: Youssef Karam dies near Naples
why: Never officially a prince; died in exile aged 65.

title: Karam's body returned to Ehden
why: Thousands gathered; he lies in a glass-topped coffin in St George's church.

title: Wasa Pasha dies in office; Naoum Pasha becomes mutasarrif
why: Wasa died eleven months before term end after corruption complaints; Naoum Coussa, nephew of Franko Pasha, governed to 1902.

title: Naoum Pasha builds over 480 km of roads and seraglios
why: Seraglios at Baakline, Jezzine, Jounieh, Batroun, Amioun and Bhannes; years given only as his tenure.

title: Large-scale emigration from Mount Lebanon marks Naoum Pasha's term
why: Source dates the start of mass departures to his 1892-1902 rule.

title: Naoum Pasha leaves; Muzaffar Pasha (Władysław Czajkowski) appointed
why: Polish Catholic count; clashed with clergy and council; to 1907.

title: Muzaffar Pasha shelves new taxes after council and clergy resist
why: Council members, backed by clergy, forced him to cancel measures; corruption claims centred on his son and wife.

title: Muzaffar Pasha dies; Yusuf Franko Pasha appointed mutasarrif
why: Son of the second mutasarrif; term 1907-1912, marked by clashes with the Administrative Council.

title: Beirut handles 11 percent of Ottoman international trade
why: Reason given for the 1888 vilayet's boom; port, road and railway fed it.

title: Yusuf Pasha tries to impose Ottoman ID cards, abolishes opposition papers
why: Strong opposition made the ID card optional.

title: First automobile reaches Beirut and drives the Sidon road
why: Came from Alexandria; crossed the Beirut-Sidon road in about 2 h 20 min.

title: Constitution restored: Young Turk Revolution celebrations begin in Istanbul
why: Restores the 1876 constitution and parliament; local rejoicing followed in provinces.

title: Beirut celebrates the constitution in the Hamidian Garden
why: Delayed two days by uncertainty; flags and banners praised the sultan and the constitution.

title: Yusuf Pasha tells Interior Ministry Lebanon will elect no deputies
why: He cited autonomy and the 1877 precedent; the Beirut vali said clergy and others had urged him not to back constitutionalists.

title: Salim Ali Salam becomes president of Beirut municipality
why: Highest post a Beirut local could reach; he later led the reform movement.

title: Delegation of about 80 asks Yusuf Pasha for reform and parliamentary seats
why: Twelve-man committee incl. Shakib Arslan, Habib al-Saad, Faris Mushriq; the mutasarrif refused to recognise them and had them removed.

title: Aley rally for constitution with CUP reform delegation and Beirut vali
why: Attendees demanded immediate elections to the Ottoman parliament; Yusuf Pasha then told qaimaqams to prepare polls.

title: Deir al-Qamar municipality telegraphs Istanbul against Lebanese elections
why: Said the privilege guaranteed by the Powers meant no obligation to send deputies; other municipalities followed.

title: Ottoman parliamentary elections; only the Shuf district in Lebanon takes part
why: Christian-majority districts refused; CUP won nearly every seat of 275, with 60 Arab deputies.

title: Thamarat al-Funun ends after 33 years; becomes al-Ittihad al-Uthmani
why: The Beirut Muslim paper of the Society of Arts closed in 1908 and reappeared as a CUP-friendly title in 1909.

title: Avnillah reduced to stationary harbour defence ship at Beirut
why: The 1869 ironclad was the main Ottoman warship in the port that Italy attacked in 1912.

title: Italy-Ottoman war begins
why: Italian fear that Ottoman ships at Beirut could threaten Suez traffic led to the 1912 strike.

title: Italian cruisers sink Ottoman ships in Beirut harbour
why: Garibaldi and Ferruccio sank the corvette Avnillah, the torpedo boat Angora and six lighters; stray shots hit the city.

title: Ottoman ultimatum expires: Italy opens fire at 09:00
why: The Vali received the surrender demand at 08:30 and was about to comply when the deadline passed.

title: Beirut bombardment kills 66 civilians, wounds hundreds
why: Fires destroyed parts of the customs house and damaged the Ottoman Bank, German Palestine Bank and Salonica Bank.

title: Ottoman crews: Avnillah loses 51-58 killed; Angora sunk at 13:45
why: Counts differ by source (2-3 officers, 49-55 men killed, 8 officers and 100 men wounded).

title: Rome officially denies Beirut city was bombarded
why: Italian admiral's report claimed only the warships were shelled; Rome called damage reports unfounded. (corrected from 1912-02-24: the NYT Rome report of 26 Feb 1912 describes the action as "yesterday"; its dateline scans as Feb 23, so the exact day is uncertain)

title: Yusuf Franko Pasha's term ends amid public resentment
why: Years of conflict with the Administrative Council ended with replacement by Ohannes Pasha.

title: Ohannes Pasha Kouyoumdjian appointed mutasarrif
why: Armenian Catholic official from the Foreign Ministry; his firman carried amendments to the Règlement.

title: 1912 firman widens council elections through delegates of 100 voters
why: Council members no longer chosen only by elders; delegates each represented one hundred voters.

title: 1912 firman allows three Lebanese ports: Jounieh, Nabi Younis, Chekka
why: A direct challenge to Beirut's port monopoly; war stopped the works.

title: Balkan war breaks out
why: Further weakened Istanbul and raised Arab demands for decentralisation.

title: Salim Salam argues for local control with European advisers
why: Article in al-Ittihad al-Uthmani a year before the Beirut Reform Society formed.

title: Beirut Reform Society inaugurated at the municipality building
why: Salim Salam and Petro Trad elected executives, Ayoub Tabet secretary; Muslims and Christians together demanded decentralisation.

title: Beirut reformers ask elected provincial council to license companies
why: Business motive: centralised Ottoman rule hindered local joint-stock projects.

title: Ottoman government closes the Beirut Reform Society
why: It did not accept the demands for local control; date within 1913 not given.

title: Young Turk coup in Istanbul precedes the Arab Congress
why: Context for centralisation and Arab reform demands.

title: First Arab Congress opens in Paris
why: Beirut Reform Society sent six delegates; five days of debate on Arab rights in the Empire.

title: Congress closes with ten resolutions
why: Official Arabic in Arab provinces, local conscription, decentralisation, wider Beirut vilayet council powers, better Lebanon finances.

title: 1913 census: Mount Lebanon 414,800 counted, 124,400 of them emigrants
why: A more reliable estimate put emigrants near 280,000, so under half were counted.

title: Najib Azuri founds Ligue de la Patrie Arabe in Paris
why: Early Arab-nationalist group aiming to free Greater Syria and Iraq from Ottoman rule.

title: Arab League Society founded in Cairo by Rashid Rida
why: Secret reform society to safeguard Arab rights.

title: Young Arab Society (al-Fatat) founded in Paris
why: Students called for the 1913 Arab Congress.

title: Ottoman Party for Administrative Decentralization founded in Cairo
why: Founded by Rafiq and Haqqi al-Azm.

title: Compagnie Impériale Ottomane de la Route Beyrouth-Damas founded
why: French-led joint-stock company with a 50-year concession; headed by Count Edmond de Perthuis.

title: Beirut-Damascus carriage road opens
why: Cut travel from about three days to thirteen hours; built by a French-Ottoman company holding a 50-year concession dated 1857 (corrected from "about eight hours" and "concession from 1863").

title: Midhat Pasha era: Beirut officials open port talks with European capital
why: Early move that led to the harbour concession of 1887.

title: Beirut port concession granted to French company
why: Compagnie du Port, des Quais et Entrepôts de Beyrouth; kept running it to 1990 under later names.

title: Gas lighting installed in Beirut
why: Gaz de Beyrouth was constituted in 1887; first city lighting reported March 1888.

title: Beirut gets a water distribution company
why: Early private utility concession in the city.

title: Firman gives Youssef Moutran Damascus tramways and Hauran rail concession
why: Sixty-year concession; later folded into the Beirut-Damascus-Hauran railway company. (corrected from 1890-04-18: source date 18 April 1890 is Julian, i.e. 30 April Gregorian)
law_no: Firman of 10 'redjeb' 1307 (as printed; 10 Ramadan 1307 = 30 Apr 1890, so 'redjeb' is likely a typo)

title: Imperial firman authorises Beirut-Damascus-Hauran economical railway company
why: Company took over the 1857 road concession in exchange for 12,500 shares; 147 km Beirut-Damascus plus 103 km Damascus-Hauran.

title: 120,000 railway bonds issued in Paris
why: Raised 31.2 million francs; 5 million lent to the Beirut port company; issued by Banque Impériale Ottomane and Société Générale.

title: Beirut port company's provisional opening planned for 1892
why: Prospectus said works to complete the harbour would allow provisional operation that year; the port moved 160,000 tonnes in six prior years.

title: Railway company gets concession for Damascus-Homs-Hama-Aleppo-Biredjik line
why: Gave the Beirut company a northern Syria network with state revenue guarantee.

title: Beirut-Damascus railway (147 km) built and opened
why: Built by Société de construction des Batignolles; French capital under an Ottoman company.

title: Ottoman iradé limits Biredjik line works to Rayak-Hama
why: Reduced the 1893 concession to 188 km with a higher revenue guarantee.

title: Railway company put in judicial liquidation after missing bond coupon
why: Seine commercial court ruled; a creditors' agreement in 1901 let it resume.

title: Railway company becomes Damascus-Hama et Prolongements (DHP), HQ Constantinople
why: Still Paris-run and French-funded.

title: Additional act extends the line from Rayak to Aleppo for 90 years
why: Total guarantee set at 13,600 francs per km per year.

title: Ottoman tramway and electricity company of Beirut founded
why: Société Anonyme Ottomane des Tramways et d'Électricité de Beyrouth held exclusive tram and power concessions.

title: Beirut electric tramway opens
why: Wikipedia dates it April 1908 and the line ran to 1960s; other sources say the company began operating in 1909.

title: Beirut tram company begins supplying electricity to selected users
why: Tram took most output; the first power plant in modern Lebanon.

title: Beirut tram and electricity company becomes mainly Belgian-owned
why: Later French-owned from 1923 and merged into the Société des Tramways et de l'Éclairage de Beyrouth by 1925.

title: Syrian Scientific Society founded in Beirut by Protestant missionaries and students
why: Early model for Beirut's cultural societies (another source dates the officers' election to 6 Jan 1852).

title: Syrian Society for Arts and Sciences elects officers
why: Its first yearbook came out of the American mission press.

title: Hadiqat al-Akhbar launched in Beirut by Khalil al-Khuri
why: First private political weekly and first Arabic paper with a regular literary section (another source says 1 Jan 1858).

title: Hadiqat al-Akhbar made semi-official at Fuad Pasha's request
why: Followed the 1860 conflict, until the official gazette Suriya began.

title: Bustani lectures on Arab literature and disengages from the mission
why: A call for Arabic revival that set the stage for the Nahda.

title: Bustani begins Nafir Suriyya pamphlets after the 1860 war
why: Eleven pamphlets to April 1861 calling for a Syrian homeland and religious tolerance.

title: W. M. Thomson proposes a Beirut college to the American Board
why: Proposal that led to the Syrian Protestant College, with Daniel Bliss as president.

title: Bustani founds the National School (al-Madrasa al-Wataniyya) in Beirut
why: Secular Arabic-led school teaching six languages and modern sciences.

title: New York State grants charter to Syrian Protestant College
why: Chartered in New York while Daniel Bliss raised funds; renamed AUB in 1920.

title: Syrian Protestant College opens in Beirut with 16 students
why: Instruction began in Arabic; Daniel Bliss was president to 1902.

title: College adds School of Medicine
why: First expansion of the Syrian Protestant College.

title: Syrian Scientific Society publishes 1868-69 proceedings with mixed membership
why: Members included Sunnis and Druze as well as Christians.

title: Bustani family launches al-Jinan, first major Arabic literary-scientific journal
why: Edited by Salim al-Bustani; al-Janna weekly followed in mid-1870.

title: Beirut press boom: over twenty periodicals launched in the 1870s
why: Includes al-Zahra, al-Nahla (Sabunji), al-Najah, al-Bashir (Jesuit) and al-Nashra.

title: Muslim Society of Arts (Jam'iyyat al-Funun) founded in Beirut
why: Educated Muslims organised to spread knowledge and help the poor.

title: Thamarat al-Funun launched by the Society of Arts
why: Weekly, Ottomanist and traditional; ran until 1908.

title: Jesuit seminary moves from Ghazir to Beirut and becomes Saint Joseph University
why: The Jesuits' first Beirut school dated from 1839; authorities allowed degrees.

title: Al-Muqtataf founded in Beirut by Sarruf and Nimr
why: Scientific monthly; moved to Cairo in 1884 and ran to 1952. (corrected from 1876-05-01: 1 May 1952 is the end date in the source table; start given as 1876 only)

title: Lisan al-Hal founded by Khalil Sarkis
why: Became a daily, the oldest Lebanese paper until it closed in 1999; censored several times under the Ottomans.

title: Lisan al-Hal first appears (month per Ayalon)
why: Semiweekly, later daily; Sarkis was Bustani's nephew.

title: Butrus al-Bustani dies in Beirut
why: Wrote Muhit al-Muhit; worked on the Van Dyck Bible translation.

title: USJ's medical institute founded
why: Became the French Faculty of Medicine in 1888 and of Medicine and Pharmacy in 1889.

title: Censorship tightens; Beirut journalists move to Egypt
why: Mass departures of Syro-Lebanese writers, including the Muqtataf team.

title: Muhammad Abduh teaches and writes in Beirut (1884-88)
why: Wrote for Thamarat al-Funun while exiled in Beirut.

title: USJ opens maternity clinic
why: Part of Jesuit medical expansion; an Oriental College followed in 1902.

title: Thamarat al-Funun gets Ahmad Tabbara as editor; Islamic reformist turn
why: Journal moved from Ottomanism to Islamic reform in the 1890s.

title: Jesuit review al-Mashriq founded
why: Listed in the 1898 Beirut periodical series.

title: Howard Bliss becomes AUB president
why: Succeeded father Daniel; served to 1920 and later advised in Paris.

title: USJ opens Oriental College
why: Part of Jesuit expansion.

title: USJ opens School for French Law and an engineering school
why: Law school under Lyon patronage; later became the Faculty of Law; AUB also began engineering courses.

title: AUB begins engineering courses
why: Engineering taught from 1913; separate school in 1951.

title: Cocoon price rises from 15 to 45 piasters per oka by 1872
why: French demand for Lebanese silk thread drove a boom that reshaped peasant income.

title: French merchants pay 45 piasters per oka of cocoons
why: Up from about 12 in the 1840s; prices held with small changes into the 1870s.

title: 33 Lebanese-run silk filatures alongside European ones
why: Rose to 101 by 1885 and 149 by 1893; ten were European-owned.

title: Bumper silk cocoon crop
why: Four years later (1870) the harvest fell below a third of normal.

title: Silk harvest falls below one third of normal
why: Volatility of Lebanese cocoon yields grew; silkworm eggs from Syria were failing by 1868.

title: Ottoman economic depression begins and lasts to 1896
why: Hit small farmers and pushed many to leave their land.

title: Silk cocoon market collapses; prices settle near 22 piasters per oka
why: East Asian silk gained after the Suez Canal cut shipping costs; prices later sank to about 19 after 1890.

title: Bad silk crop year, repeated 1877, 1879, 1885, 1891, 1895, 1909
why: Peasants who had borrowed against the harvest went bankrupt.

title: Silk cocoons make 38 percent of Mount Lebanon income
why: Wheat came second at about 21 percent; in 1906 Metn silk gave about 82 percent of district revenue.

title: About 12,000 of 14,000 filature workers in Mount Lebanon are women
why: Lebanese male workers earned about 40 percent of French wages, women about 22 percent.

title: Silk crisis: cheaper Asian silk floods European markets
why: Silk was around 60 percent of Mount Lebanon's economy by 1900; its fall fuelled emigration.

title: Silk worth over 42 million piasters to Mount Lebanon
why: About 60 percent of a peasant family's income; olive oil and sheep together were under 29 million.

title: French advance about 8 million francs a year to Lebanese filatures
why: Sum equal to just over a third of the silk they bought there.

title: Antonios Bishallany reaches the US, first 19th-century Arab immigrant named
why: Isolated early arrival; mass emigration came decades later.

title: Two men from the Lebanese coast leave for the US
why: Names unknown; only a few hundred Lebanese emigrated before 1887.

title: Emigration to the Americas jumps to hundreds a year
why: Mostly to US, Brazil and Argentina; by the mid-1890s thousands a year.

title: Beirut police cover for an illegal emigrant shipment on the Foria
why: 101 Syrians and 36 Armenians boarded; the probe found a network that moved 5,000+ people out over two decades.

title: Beirut police chief reports crowds boarding for other Ottoman ports
why: He said emigrants held valid permits and he could not stop them.

title: Ottoman state lifts ban on Syrian emigration
why: After the Beirut governor's advice; yearly emigrants then rose from hundreds to thousands.

title: Ellis Island records change origin label from Turkey to Syria after 1899
why: Immigrants entered as Syrians; between the 1870s and 1930s some 120,000 immigrants left the Eastern Mediterranean for the US (corrected from 1899 date and from an unsupported "60,000 census" count; source says Syria replaced Turkey in Asia for most entries after 1900).

title: About 90,000 leave Mount Lebanon for the US per Ellis Island records
why: Estimate; return flows unknown. By 1910 about 3,000 Lebanese lived in Lawrence, Massachusetts.

title: About 131,000 leave for Argentina, 83,000 return
why: Round-trip movement; Argentina got 132,000 Middle Easterners in 1897-1914 versus 3,733 in 1880-96.

title: Cumulative emigration by 1914: US 106,424, Argentina 136,060, Brazil 55,954
why: Counts from US, Argentine and Brazilian records cited by Khater.

title: Mount Lebanon population under 300,000; over 500,000 by 1911
why: Vaccination and improved health nearly doubled it, outpacing local jobs.

title: About 280,000 emigrants from Mount Lebanon
why: Roughly 45 percent of Mountain residents left between 1860 and 1914 per one estimate.

title: Beirut about 140,000 people; Damascus about 200,000
why: Context for the French road: it linked the two largest Syrian centres.

title: Tanzimat reforms first applied in Beirut
why: Followed by a second wave after the 1860 conflict.

title: Port of Beirut constructed 1887-1890 with French capital
why: Port made Beirut a transit city for re-export of European goods; city grew from ~10,000 to over 100,000.

title: Mutasarrif Wasa Pasha faces objections to new judiciary system
why: Cassation court moved to Constantinople, seen as breach of the Règlement (exact year within 1883-92 not given).
